title: Connecting Cities With Minimum Cost
statement:
There are `n` cities labelled `1` to `n`. Each entry `connections[i] = [xi, yi, costi]` offers a road between cities `xi` and `yi` that can be built for `costi`; a built road can be travelled in both directions. The same pair of cities may be offered more than once.

Choose roads to build so that every city can reach every other city through built roads, and return the smallest possible total cost of the chosen roads. If even building every offered road leaves some city unreachable, return `-1`.
notes:
## Intuition

The cheapest way to connect every city never contains a cycle: dropping any road from a cycle keeps everything connected and costs no more. So the answer is the weight of a minimum spanning tree. Kruskal's rule builds one greedily: take roads from cheapest to most expensive and keep a road only when it joins two cities that are not yet connected. A union-find structure answers "already connected?" almost instantly. If the roads run out before everything is one group, no plan exists.

## Approach

1. Give every city its own group: `parent[city] = city`. `find` walks up to a group's root, halving the path as it goes.
2. Sort a copy of the roads by cost into `edges`.
3. Keep `total` (cost so far) and `groups` (number of separate groups, starting at `n`).
4. For each road `[x, y, cost]`, find `rootX` and `rootY`. If they match, the road would close a cycle, so skip it.
5. Otherwise merge the groups, add `cost` to `total` and decrease `groups`. Once `groups` is 1, return `total`.
6. If the loop ends with more than one group, return `-1`.

## Example 1, step by step

Sorted roads: `[2,3,1]`, `[1,2,5]`, `[1,3,6]`. Road 2–3 joins two groups: `total = 1`, `groups = 2`. Road 1–2 joins city 1 to the group of 2 and 3: `total = 6`, `groups = 1`, so the answer is `6`. Road 1–3 is never needed.

## Complexity

- Time: O(m log m) for sorting the m roads; the union-find work is nearly linear.
- Space: O(n + m) for `parent` and the sorted copy.

## Pitfalls

- Cities are numbered from 1, so `parent` needs `n + 1` slots.
- Being out of roads is not the only failure: check that exactly one group remains before returning `total`.
- Merge the roots, not the cities themselves, or groups silently split apart.
- Costs can be 0; a zero-cost road still has to be counted as joining two groups.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `parent` | union-find parent of each city; a root is its own parent |
| `find` | returns the root of a city's group |
| `edges` | the roads sorted by cost |
| `total` | cost of the roads kept so far |
| `groups` | how many separate groups of cities remain |
| `rootX`, `rootY` | roots of the two ends of the current road |

narration.2: Every city starts as the root of its own group; index 0 is unused.
narration.4: Climb towards the root until a city is its own parent.
narration.5: Path halving: point this city at its grandparent so later searches are shorter.
narration.11: Sort a copy of the roads so the cheapest are tried first.
narration.13: Before any road is built, every city is its own group.
narration.15: Consider the roads from cheapest to most expensive.
narration.18: Both ends already share a root, so this road would only close a cycle.
narration.21: Join the two groups by hanging one root under the other.
narration.22: Pay for the road that was just kept.
narration.24: Once a single group remains, every city is connected.
narration.25: No cheaper plan exists, so return the cost now.
narration.28: The roads ran out; return -1 unless everything ended up in one group.
